hero.kicker: A daily AI/ML brief that can prove it isn't making things up
hero.title: I stopped trying to keep up.
hero.titleAccent: So I built something that decides what's worth knowing.
hero.lede: Five minutes a morning. The fewest items I'd regret missing — not the most items covered. Every factual claim traced back to its source by code, not by a model's promise.

sections.title: Twenty minutes a day, and I still felt behind

blocks.html: Every morning I opened five to ten tabs of AI/ML news and closed them twenty minutes later knowing roughly what I knew before. Not because the writing was bad — because almost none of it told me whether I should care.

A model shipped. A benchmark moved two points. Somebody raised a round. Every item arrived with the same breathless weight as every other item, and the work of deciding which ones mattered to my work fell entirely on me, at 7am, before coffee.
The real cost was never the twenty minutes. It was walking into a conversation three weeks later and finding that something I'd scrolled past had quietly become the thing everyone was building on.
So the problem wasn't "I don't have enough information." It was "I have far too much, and no reliable way to separate signal from noise in the time I actually have."

sections.title: The obvious fixes each fail in their own way

blocks.title: Curated newsletters
blocks.body: Written for a general audience, so relevance is a coincidence — and they need something exciting every single day, which is exactly the pressure that manufactures noise.

blocks.title: Aggregators and feeds
blocks.body: Solved distribution, not judgement. I still had to read everything to find the two things that mattered.

blocks.title: Asking a chatbot
blocks.body: Fast, fluent, and no way to know when it was wrong. A summary you can't verify is worse than none — it feels like knowledge.

blocks.title: Save it for later
blocks.body: Later never came. The reading list became its own source of guilt rather than a solution to any.

blocks.html: Success is the fewest items I'd regret missing — not the most items covered. The system is explicitly allowed to say "quiet day, go build something", and that is a correct answer rather than a failure.

That one decision changed everything downstream. A system optimising for coverage wants to show you more. A system optimising for regret wants to show you less, and has to be far more confident about whatever survives.

sections.title: A funnel, ending in something you'll actually read

blocks.html: Everything reachable gets narrowed to a handful of items, each with the one thing that makes it matter to me and the tradeoff it implies — plus the thread connecting the day, which is usually the part worth knowing.
Once a week it goes further and turns something from the brief into a 60-minute exercise grounded in my own repositories. Reading becomes doing, or it doesn't count.

sections.title: How do I know it didn't make that up?

blocks.html: Writing a readable brief is the easy half. The half that took the work has nothing to do with news: a summariser that occasionally invents a figure isn't mildly flawed — it makes you confidently wrong in public.
So the model is never trusted to verify itself. Three layers, each checking something the one before it can't.

blocks.caption: A model can invent a quote. A substring check cannot be talked into agreeing.
blocks.svg: <svg style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block" viewBox="0 0 640 172" role="img" aria-label="Three layers: a model writes, a second model checks, code proves the evidence is real"><line x1="8" y1="44" x2="632" y2="44" stroke="#201c17" stroke-opacity="0.12"/><text x="8" y="26" font-family="ui-monospace,Menlo,monospace" font-size="10" letter-spacing="1.8" fill="#8a8071">WRITES</text><text x="8" y="74" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="14.5" fill="#201c17">A model drafts the brief</text><text x="8" y="96" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12.5" fill="#5f584c">Given only each item's source</text><text x="8" y="113" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12.5" fill="#5f584c">excerpt to draw facts from.</text><line x1="222" y1="34" x2="222" y2="152" stroke="#201c17" stroke-opacity="0.12"/><text x="244" y="26" font-family="ui-monospace,Menlo,monospace" font-size="10" letter-spacing="1.8" fill="#8a8071">CHECKS</text><text x="244" y="74" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="14.5" fill="#201c17">A second model audits it</text><text x="244" y="96" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12.5" fill="#5f584c">Lists every factual claim and</text><text x="244" y="113" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12.5" fill="#5f584c">must quote what supports it.</text><line x1="432" y1="34" x2="432" y2="152" stroke="#201c17" stroke-opacity="0.12"/><text x="454" y="26" font-family="ui-monospace,Menlo,monospace" font-size="10" letter-spacing="1.8" fill="#b5502a">PROVES</text><text x="454" y="74" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="14.5" fill="#b5502a">Code verifies the quote</text><text x="454" y="96" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12.5" fill="#5f584c">Not literally in the source?</text><text x="454" y="113" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12.5" fill="#5f584c">The claim is rejected — whatever</text><text x="454" y="130" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12.5" fill="#5f584c">the auditor concluded.</text></svg>

blocks.html: That third layer exists because of something the second one did. Asked to justify a fabricated figure, the auditing model produced a quote supporting it — a quote that appeared nowhere in the source. It had invented a citation.

And because the auditor is a model too, it gets its own test suite: one day of real output frozen with hand-written labels, re-run on every change. Its first version passed a brief I had deliberately seeded with a fake valuation, a fake date and a fake investor — a scoping bug meant it had never read the writing it was auditing. A test that has never failed is not evidence of anything.

sections.title: One agent of six actually runs

blocks.html: The brief you'll see is real output — genuinely what the agent produced — but from a hand-built input pool on a fixed date. Live ingestion starts with the next phase. The full built-versus-designed breakdown is in Plan & Progress.

The slice that exists was chosen deliberately rather than by convenience: the agent whose output a human actually reads, and the harness that can stop it from shipping. Everything else is easier once those two exist, and far harder to retrofit afterwards.
